rv.q: In every detail, the production is crisp and precise yet emotionally penetrating, just as the play and its central character demand.

The humor in Nixon's play is grim, grim, grim and Nixon – along with director Lynne Meadow, who are both cancer survivors – have wrung out every ounce in a 100-minute, intermission-less production...In a play about ultimately reconnecting with one's humanity, Nixon is almost too hard to watch at the end.
Her outer Bearing is more of a pose, a defensive posture; but her inner bearing is incandescent.
This is a performance that is large and lucid and delicate at the same time, and it justifies Manhattan Theater Club’s decision to mount what is essentially a chamber piece on Broadway.

Intellectual sarcasm is simply not the forte of this likable thesp, and she’s not at her best in these early slash-and-burn scenes when Vivian is desperately drawing on the strength of her towering intellect to see her through the non-poetic realities of her oncoming death.

Nixon takes care of the furniture. She's respectful, reliable and committed... But Nixon also has a certain solemn, brittle coldness — the humorous lines in this surprisingly funny play don't always land — and keeps the audience at arm's length.
The doctors are especially cruel clunks against a Vivian who cannot keep her lamby sweetness from twinkling under her tough skin.
Still, it’s a testament to this remarkable play and Nixon’s skill that we ultimately believe her as the cancer-stricken teacher.
Ms. McDonald's performance is nothing short of extraordinary.
Fearless doesn't even begin to describe Nixon's performance.
For Nixon's part, she doesn't perform as much as live the character; you get the feeling they've imported her from a real hospital ward, where she has walked and lived the talk.
Nixon deserves a lot of credit for taking on such an unglamorous role.
It's hard to imagine anyone but Kathleen Chalfant as the overbearing but brilliant Dr. Vivian Bearing.
Indeed it is Vivian’s acceptance, her ability to find spiritual fulfillment that makes “Wit” a theatrical treasure.
In a play about ultimately reconnecting with one's humanity, Nixon is almost too hard to watch at the end.
She gives a commanding performance, one in which hard, sharp edges subtly soften.
Nixon has given numerous first-rate performances in contemporary fare – at this same theatre, she etched a fine portrait of motherly grief in Rabbit Hole.

cn.t: Critics praise this elegant Broadway revival of Edson's Pulitzer-winning drama, with Cynthia Nixon delivering a shattering, commanding performance that masterfully balances the play's delicate opposites of clinical detachment and raw human emotion.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
